messages.body_plain:
Hi folks, looking for advice on testing the following (and whether it's possible in mirt):

I have an ability test with 9 binary (correct/incorrect) items, best modeled as a bifactor (3 group factors with 3 items each, plus a general).  The test was administered twice, and we find that people do better on the second administration (no surprise) on all items but 1.  The factor structure and loadings remain the same on both administrations, so this seems to me like a case of longitudinal uniform DIF (for that one item that didn't get easier on second administration).  My question is, how do I test this?  The combination of bifactor framework and dependent (repeated) measures seems like a minefield for specification errors.  Any help would be appreciated.

Thanks in advance!

Tyler

Thanks for the clarification, I have tried out and works as expected.
I did some additional research, and even though I do not understand in details yet why the information for 3PL is not equivalent to the second derivative of the log likelihood, I have tried to replicate the result found with the 2PL and ML estimation for 3PL.

I found out that there is a small difference between the Information calculated with testinfo and the one obtained with the following (the source is the book called 'Educational Measurements'):

1) Could you please explain the reason why?

2) Also, could you also explain why the testinfo function returns a different value from the inverse of the cube of the SE obtained from fscore?

3) Finally, could you please confirm that the formula used for SE computation in EAP is formula [5] from Bock, R. D., & Mislevy, R. J. (1982). Adaptive EAP estimation of ability in a microcomputer environment. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6, 431-444 ?

Thank you in advance.

Here is the code I ran
library(mirt)
library(stats4)
library(lattice)

model <- 'F = 1-5
          PRIOR = (5, g, norm, -1.5, 3)'

info_3PL <- function(a, c, prob) {
  Q <- 1-prob
  P <- prob
  res <- a ^ 2 * Q / P * ((P-c)/(1-c))^2
  return(res)
}

info_2PL <- function(a, prob) {
  Q <- 1-prob
  P <- prob
  res <- a^2*P*Q
  return(res)
}

prob_2PL <- function(a,d,theta){
  res <- 1/(1+ exp(-a*(theta+d)))
  return(res)
}

prob_3PL <- function(a,d,c,theta){
  res = c + (1-c) * prob_2PL(a,d,theta)
  return(res)
}

derivative_3PL <- function(a,d,c,theta){
   num <- a^2 * (c-1) * exp(a*theta + d) * ( exp(2*(a*theta+d)) - c )
   den <- (exp(a*theta + d) + 1)^2 * (exp(a*theta + d) + c)^2
   res = -1 * num / den
   return(res)
}

data <- expand.table(LSAT7)
modfisher3PL <- mirt(data, model, '3PL', TOL=0.0001,SE=T)
scoresfisher3PL = fscores(modfisher3PL, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE>=T, method='ML')

params3PL = coef(modfisher3PL)

info3PL = testinfo(modfisher3PL, scoresfisher3PL[,1])
se3PL = 1./sqrt(info3PL[400])
print(paste('se using 1/sqrt', se3PL))
print(paste('se using testinfo', scoresfisher3PL[400, 2]))
# SE calculated with 1/sqrt is lower than SE returned from fscores
# That means that the info from testinfo is higher than the one used in ML
reversed_info3PL = (1/scoresfisher3PL[400,2])^2
print(paste('info from (1/SE)^2', reversed_info3PL))
print(paste('info from testinfo', info3PL[400]))

# For item 2, let's check the second derivative against
# the FI calculated with testinfo and against the FI calculated with formula
item2_fi_3PL <- testinfo(modfisher3PL, scoresfisher3PL[,1][400], which.items = 2)
prob_400_student_3PL <- prob_3PL(
  params3PL$Item.2['par','a1'],
  params3PL$Item.2['par','d'],
  params3PL$Item.2['par','g'],
  scoresfisher3PL[,1][400]
)
fi_3PL <- info_3PL(params3PL$Item.2['par','a1'],params3PL$Item.2['par','g'], prob_400_student_3PL)

der <- derivative_3PL(params3PL$Item.2['par','a1'],
                      params3PL$Item.2['par','d'],
                      params3PL$Item.2['par','g'],
                      scoresfisher3PL[,1][400])

print(paste('info with testinfo for item 2',item2_fi_3PL))
print(paste('info with formula for item 2', fi_3PL))
print(paste('derivative log likelihood for item 2', der))

# Check test info for student number 400
sum <- 0
for (x in seq(length(params3PL) - 1)){
  item <- params3PL[x]
  prob_400_student_3PL <- prob_3PL(
    item$Item['par','a1'],
    item$Item['par','d'],
    item$Item['par','g'],
    scoresfisher3PL[,1][400]
  )
  sum <- sum + info_3PL(item$Item['par','a1'], item$Item['par','g'], prob_400_student_3PL)
}
print(paste('total info from sum of single items', sum))
print(paste('total info from testinfo', info3PL[400]))

messages.body_plain:
The determinant of the observed information matrix is required for WLEs, which is a bit of a limitation. If there isn't sufficient information in the pattern of the factor loadings/slopes given the observed response pattern then this may not be computable. It's similar to the issue of MLE estimation, but occurs for a different reason. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: bifactor model within item dimensionality
messages.body_plain:
More complex loading patterns make the dimension reduction technique used in the bfactor() function less optimal, though it can be done through the two-tier estimation approach. What you would want to do is specify the orthogonal specific factor patterns, as you showed before, and modify the model input to add in the more complex loading patterns (general + other specific loadings). The downside is that more numerical integrals will be required, but this should still be more optimal than using functions like mirt(), even with stochastic estimation methods. There are some examples in ?bfactor which demonstrate two-tier analyses (see Li Cai's publications for more information on this topic). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: longitudinal DIF in bifactor
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

In this situation you could setup the test via the multipleGroup() function to allow constraining the slope/intercept parameters for all items (sans the item that you suspect to have DIF), and compare it to the nested model which would constrain all slope/intercepts to be equal. I would recommend this approach over the group input to bfactor() because this way you can freely estimate the mean/variances of the focal group parameters to allow for proper parameter linking across all latent traits, whereas in bfactor() such estimation approaches are not possible due to the dimensional reduction technique. HTH.

Phil

Hi Phil, I'm reading your 2016 paper "It might not make a big DIF..." (it is awesome by the way). I'd like to use the method you discuss for evaluating DIF but want to be sure I'm translating your method to its programming in mirt correctly. I've copied and pasted your methods and the coding for each step below. Does this look right to you? (this example assumes the test is 10 items and has 5-point response cats). Thank you so much!

1. "To establish a set of potential anchor items, we used a multigroup GRM with no across-group equality constraints as a reference model.
mod1 <- multipleGroup(data = df[,c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5", "x6", "x7, "x8", "x9", "x10")], 1, itemtype = "graded", group = as.character(df[,11]), invariance = c('free_means', 'free_var'), SE = TRUE)
2. "Next, likelihood-ratio tests were used to compare the reference model to models that added across-group equality constraints to the a and dk parameters one item at a time. To account for the large number of likelihood ratio tests, we used the multiplicity control method of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). Based on the DIF analysis, we determined that the third, sixth, seventh, and eighth items were invariant across the two countries. "

> dif <- DIF(mod1, c('a', "d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"), scheme = 'add_sequential',  p.adjust = 'BH', seq_stat = .01)

3. "Therefore, these items were used as anchor items in the final multigroup IRT model so that the latent mean and variance parameters in the German group could be estimated. A likelihood-ratio test comparing our final model to a multigroup IRT model with no across-group equality constraints was not statistically significant."
mod2 <- multipleGroup(data = df[,"x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5", "x6", "x7, "x8", "x9", "x10")], 1, itemtype = "graded", group = as.character(df[,11]), invariance = c('x3', 'x6', 'x7', 'x8', 'free_means', 'free_var'), SE = TRUE)
dif2 <- DIF(mod2, c('a', "d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"), scheme = 'drop',  items2test = c(1:2,4:5,9:10))
Thank you again! -Jeannie
